questions.questionText: Why don't precision/recall/F1 from the Classical ML course directly apply to evaluating most LLM output?
options: They apply exactly the same way, no changes needed
Free-form text usually has no single well-defined "correct answer" to check equality against, unlike a classification label
LLMs never produce text that can be evaluated at all
Those metrics only work for regression tasks
questions.correctAnswer: Free-form text usually has no single well-defined "correct answer" to check equality against, unlike a classification label
questions.explanation: Classification metrics assume a fixed correct label to compare against; free-form generation (summaries, explanations, conversation) typically has many valid phrasings, so different evaluation approaches are needed.

questions.questionText: What is a known risk of using LLM-as-judge for evaluation?
options: It's completely unbiased and needs no validation
Judge models have their own biases (e.g. favoring longer or stylistically familiar responses) and need clear rubrics plus periodic human spot-checks
It can only be used for code generation tasks
It requires no criteria or rubric to work well
questions.correctAnswer: Judge models have their own biases (e.g. favoring longer or stylistically familiar responses) and need clear rubrics plus periodic human spot-checks
questions.explanation: LLM judges scale evaluation well but aren't a free pass — they need specific criteria to check against and should be periodically validated against actual human judgment.

questions.questionText: Why is a fixed eval set of representative test cases more reliable than judging "does this prompt change feel better" informally?
options: It isn't more reliable, informal judgment is just as good
It turns an easily-biased subjective impression into a measurable, comparable pass rate across consistent test cases, avoiding cherry-picked examples
Eval sets remove the need for any evaluation criteria
Eval sets only work for classification models, not LLMs
questions.correctAnswer: It turns an easily-biased subjective impression into a measurable, comparable pass rate across consistent test cases, avoiding cherry-picked examples
questions.explanation: This mirrors the Classical ML course's train/test discipline: a consistent, fixed evaluation set makes it possible to objectively compare changes instead of relying on a potentially biased spot-check of a few examples.
